MELINOE: Fine-Tuning Enables Memory-Efficient Inference for Mixture-of-Experts Models

Arian Raje (araje@andrew.cmu.edu) Affiliation: Dept. of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Carnegie Mellon University    Anupam Nayak Affiliation: Dept. of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Carnegie Mellon University    Gauri Joshi Affiliation: Dept. of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Carnegie Mellon University
Abstract

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model architectures can significantly reduce the number of activated parameters per token, enabling computationally efficient training and inference. However, their large overall parameter counts and model sizes have precluded their widespread usage in resource-constrained settings as all of the parameters must still be loaded into GPU memory. Prior works aim to address this memory bottleneck by offloading certain experts into CPU memory and porting them to GPU memory only when they are activated. In practice, these methods suffer from the significant I/O latency incurred by expert transfer. We present melinoe, a method that fine-tunes an MoE model to more strongly prefer activating a smaller number of experts per sequence. Caching these preferred experts in GPU memory reduces expert churn and CPU-GPU transfer overhead. melinoe increases throughput by 1.21.2–3×3\times over efficient baselines and up to 14.7×14.7\times over transfer-heavy baselines while retaining or even improving the performance of the model on a downstream task, making it a reliable method for improving MoE inference efficiency.

1  Introduction

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are a Large Language Model (LLM) architecture that aim to reduce the per-token computational cost of training and inference. MoEs achieve this reduction in compute by fragmenting the traditionally dense Feed Forward Network (FFN) layer in the model architecture into a sparsely gated set of multiple FFNs, referred to as “experts” [25, 18, 11]. This reparameterization of the FFN used in transformer-based architectures makes MoE models an efficient alternative to their traditional dense counterparts. MoE models have become the flagship models for open-source model developers [15] or have been offered as an alternative to dense transformers in a model suite [22, 1, 5]. However, these gains do not come for free; while MoEs execute only a fraction of their parameters per token, their total parameter footprint remains large. During autoregressive generation, any expert may be routed to at any given step, so the corresponding expert’s weights must be resident in GPU memory prior to its activation.

The necessary residency of experts in GPU memory prior to activation results in one of two scenarios. First, all experts are simultaneously loaded into GPU memory, which can be prohibitive in resource-constrained settings with limited memory. This regime is also wasteful since only a small subset of experts is used per token, yet many unused expert parameters still occupy GPU memory. An alternative paradigm is where only a small subset of the total experts is kept in GPU memory while the remaining experts are offloaded into CPU memory [10, 31, 39]. The GPU resident experts constitute an expert cache, and experts are fetched from CPU memory on demand when selected by the router. While this reduces peak GPU memory usage, it introduces a new bottleneck. Frequent expert swaps incur substantial Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) transfer latency and can stall generation when the required expert is not already cached. The resulting churn can dominate end-to-end inference latency, especially when expert routing is diverse across tokens causing frequent transfers. When GPU memory is especially constrained, these problems are exacerbated as only a limited number of experts can be retained in the GPU-resident expert cache (Table 1).

Prior methods propose a variety of alternative approaches to balancing memory efficiency and I/O latency. Mixtral-Offloading [10] offloads most experts to CPU DRAM and keeps a small per-layer GPU-resident expert cache. However, I/O slowdowns still hinder improvements in end-to-end inference latency. Their aggressive mixed-precision quantization also trades model quality for memory efficiency. MoE-Infinity [31] and FLoE [39] seek to reduce I/O transfers by using sophisticated prefetching techniques to predict which experts will be activated prior to the router selecting them. Yet, their gains depend on prediction accuracy and routing locality, where a subset of experts are activated with high probability for consecutive tokens, so diverse routing could still trigger a significant number of cache misses and evictions. Fiddler [16] reduces PCIe traffic by executing some expert computation on the CPU, but its gains are contingent on CPU capability and diminish as per-expert token counts grow, where CPU execution becomes slow and weight transfers to GPU become preferable. Meaningfully, several prior systems do not directly target reducing the number of CPU–GPU transfers, which can be a dominant cost in resource-constrained MoE inference. In other words, prior work largely treats routing as fixed and optimizes around it via prefetching, offloading, or quantization. An alternative perspective is to treat routing as malleable and directly shape expert activation patterns.

In this vein, we present Mixture-of-Experts with Lightweight Inference and Network Offloading Efficiency, melinoe, a framework that targets the number of CPU-GPU transfers in MoE offloading applications to reduce the amount of I/O overhead. With melinoe, the model is fine-tuned with an auxiliary loss function that penalizes the model for inducing excessive cache transfers. This fine-tuning procedure occurs prior to deploying the MoE model in a memory-constrained system. Since individual sequences already have slight expert preferences, fine-tuning tilts the model towards using a small subset of experts more heavily while retaining or improving the performance of the model on a downstream task. melinoe then employs an MLP-based predictor to forecast these preferred experts prior to decoding, making prefetching more reliable since activated experts are less diverse per sequence. melinoe can improve throughput measured by tokens/s by 1.21.2–3×3\times over efficient baselines and up to 14.7×14.7\times over transfer-heavy baselines across model architectures and hardware configurations, demonstrating its reliability and robustness. Notably, since the fine-tuning procedure is orthogonal to prior offloading techniques, it composes naturally with other baselines and improves their effectiveness. melinoe provides a practical path to MoE deployment by fine-tuning the model to reduce I/O latency without sacrificing model quality.

2  Problem Setup and Motivation

MoE models replace the dense FFN in each transformer block with a sparsely gated set of FFN “experts”. For each token in the sequence, a router selects a subset of experts to execute, producing token-level activations, while the remaining experts are inactive. We denote by 𝐄(ℓ)\mathbf{E}^{(\ell)} the set of experts in the MoE layer ℓ∈[1⋯L]\ell\in[1\cdots L]. Let E:=|𝐄(ℓ)|∀ℓ∈[1⋯L]E:=|\mathbf{E}^{(\ell)}|\;\forall\ell\in[1\cdots L]. Individual experts in this layer are indexed as 𝐄i(ℓ)\mathbf{E}^{(\ell)}_{i}, where i∈{1,⋯E}i\in\{1,\cdots E\}. The output of the ℓ\ell-th MoE layer for an input 𝐱in∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is given by

𝐩(ℓ)=softmax⁡(𝐖r(ℓ)​𝐱in),𝐫(ℓ)=Top​-​K​(𝐩(ℓ)),\mathbf{p}^{(\ell)}\;=\;\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{r}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}}\right),\ \mathbf{r}^{(\ell)}=\;\mathrm{Top}\text{-}K\!\left(\mathbf{p}^{(\ell)}\right),
𝐲=∑𝐫i(ℓ)=1𝐩i(ℓ)​𝐄i(ℓ)​(𝐱in).\mathbf{y}\;=\;\sum_{\mathbf{r}^{(\ell)}_{i}=1}\mathbf{p}_{i}^{(\ell)}\,\mathbf{E}^{(\ell)}_{i}(\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}}). (1)

Here, 𝐖r(ℓ)∈ℝE×d\mathbf{W}_{r}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times d} denotes the router weight matrix at layer ℓ\ell. The Top​-​K\mathrm{Top}\text{-}K operator selects the KK experts with the highest routing probabilities, setting the corresponding entries of 𝐫(ℓ)\mathbf{r}^{(\ell)} to 11 and masking all remaining experts. Thus, ‖𝐫(ℓ)‖1=K\|\mathbf{r}^{(\ell)}\|_{1}=K . The layer output is then computed by activating only the selected experts, as shown in Equation (1).

The hyperparameter KK controls the number of experts activated per token and is model-specific, for example K=2K=2 in Mixtral-8x7B. For hidden dimension dd and intermediate dimension dffd_{\mathrm{ff}}, each expert is implemented as an MLP with three linear projections: a gate (𝐖g,i(ℓ)∈ℝdff×d)\left(\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{g,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{ff}}\times d}\right), an up (𝐖u,i(ℓ)∈ℝdff×d)\left(\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{u,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{ff}}\times d}\right), and a down (𝐖d,i(ℓ)∈ℝd×dff)\left(\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{d,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{\mathrm{ff}}}\right) projection. The forward computation of expert ii at layer ℓ\ell is

𝐄i(ℓ)​(𝐱in)=𝐖d,i(ℓ)​(ϕ⁡(𝐖g,i(ℓ)​(𝐱in))⊙𝐖u,i(ℓ)​(𝐱in)).\mathbf{E}_{i}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}})\;=\;\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{d,i}\Big(\phi\!\left(\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{g,i}(\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}})\right)\odot\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{u,i}(\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}})\Big). (2)

where ⊙\odot is an element-wise product and ϕ\phi is the gate nonlinearity. Although only a few experts are evaluated per token, the expert parameters dominate the model’s memory footprint. In OLMoE, the experts constitute 93%93\% of the weights in the model, and in Mixtral-8x7B, the experts make up 96%96\%. This discordance between expert activations and their memory footprint motivates offloading applications.

Expert Offloading Systems.

Prior works mitigate MoE model’s memory requirements by storing most expert weights in CPU DRAM and keeping only a small subset resident in GPU VRAM as an expert cache. During decoding, when the router selects an expert that is not currently resident, the system must fetch that expert’s weights from DRAM and transfer them over the CPU–GPU interconnect, typically PCIe, into VRAM before the expert can be executed on the GPU. End-to-end decoding time therefore includes both GPU computation and transfer-induced stalls

Timedecode≈Timecompute+Nmiss⋅Timetransfer\text{Time}_{\text{decode}}\;\approx\;\text{Time}_{\text{compute}}\;+\;N_{\text{miss}}\;\cdot\;\text{Time}_{\text{transfer}} (3)

where NmissN_{\text{miss}} refers to the number of cache misses where the desired expert is not currently stored in GPU VRAM. Since expert weights dominate the model’s parameter count, even modest cache budgets can lead to substantial transfer overhead. In many cases, NmissN_{\text{miss}} can reach tens of thousands even over short generations (Figure 1(a)). During pretraining, load balancing objectives encourage broad expert utilization, a beneficial goal in batched, multi-GPU settings to ensure experts on different devices take roughly the same amount of time to execute. However, such objectives increase the number of distinct experts touched during generation, escalating the number of transfers from the expert cache.

Expert Specialization.

While standard load balancing objectives spread the probability mass of expert activations across many experts, empirical evidence suggests that MoE routing is not arbitrary. Within a given sequence, the router typically exhibits a consistent but weak preference for a subset of experts, indicating a degree of sequence-level specialization [20, 14, 29]. This suggests that some experts contribute disproportionately to a sequence’s computation for a given prompt, even if the router still routes a nontrivial fraction of tokens elsewhere. However, in pretrained models this preference is too marginal to yield large gains from naïve caching. Even if we keep the “most preferred” experts in GPU VRAM, they may account for only a modest fraction of the total activations within a sequence, so cache hit rates remain limited. For example, with OLMoE we observe that, on average, the top 88 experts by activation within a sequence account for only ∼31%\sim 31\% of expert activations (Figure 1(b)). Even though this is still greater than the expected activation rate of 12.5%12.5\% from all experts being activated equally, it still leaves substantial routing mass on experts that have been offloaded into CPU DRAM. Ultimately, the practical value of these preferred experts in offloading systems is paltry.

Fine-Tuning to Achieve Cache-Friendliness.

Nevertheless, the observation of preferred experts motivates an important question: to what extent can we increase the concentration of expert usage within a sequence to improve expert-cache hit rates? Specifically, since the model already has a set of preferred experts per sequence, tilting the model’s routing decisions towards these experts could amplify its natural per-sequence preferences. By tilting routing towards a more consistent set of experts within each sequence, we increase routing locality and make VRAM caching substantially more effective by reducing cache churn.

A few considerations are critical for making this approach work in practice. First, we must design an auxiliary objective that encourages the router to reuse a smaller set of experts within a sequence, increasing routing locality and reducing the number of transfers. At the same time, fine-tuning must preserve the base model’s quality. A key failure mode that would impair the model’s expressiveness is router collapse where the same subset of experts become the preferred experts globally. Here, the remaining experts would not contribute to the model’s predictions, degrading the fine-tuned model’s integrity. The desired behavior is sequence-specific skew, where expert preferences should be persistent over the course of decoding for a given input but should vary across inputs. Finally, once such per-sequence structure is induced, we need a reliable way to predict the preferred experts before decoding begins. Accurate prediction enables proactive caching of these experts in GPU memory, making the cache substantially more effective because the same experts are likely to remain useful throughout generation. Thus, we have the following desiderata for melinoe:

  • •

    Auxiliary Loss for Routing Locality: A practical fine-tuning procedure for offloading needs an objective that penalizes too broad expert utilization per sequence.

  • •

    Global Expert Usage Diversity: Expert usage should remain diverse across sequences to preserve the model’s performance and prevent expert starvation.

  • •

    Expert Activation Prediction: Once the model has been fine-tuned and subsequently deployed on a memory-constrained device, there must be a mechanism for predicting per-sequence expert activations based on the prompt.

3  Method

We present melinoe, a practical expert-offloading recipe that reduces end-to-end inference latency. We structure the method into two stages, namely pre- and post-deployment, because the resources available to a model provider differ fundamentally before and after releasing a model to a memory-constrained device. In the pre-deployment stage, the provider can access the full-precision MoE weights as well as fine-tuning data. We leverage this setting to (i) fine-tune the MoE with an auxiliary objective that increases per-sequence routing locality (Section 3.1.1) and (ii) train an activation predictor that anticipates which experts will be most useful for a given input (Section 3.1.2). In the post-deployment stage, the model is executed under tight VRAM budgets. Here, we use the trained predictor to proactively pre-load a GPU-resident expert cache before decoding begins for every sequence. Once these experts have been prefetched, we perform standard offloaded inference with substantially fewer transfers during generation (Section 3.2).

3.1  Pre-Deployment Stage

3.1.1  MoE Fine-Tuning Procedure

melinoe hinges on the following auxiliary fine-tuning objectives that we use to reshape routing behavior. We simplify notation for the purpose of improved readability.

Cache Simulation Loss ℒc​s\mathcal{L}_{cs}.

The first auxiliary objective is a cache simulation loss that directly penalizes routing patterns likely to induce expert transfers under a memory budget. We denote the router distribution for token t∈[1,…,T]t\in[1,\ldots,T] at layer ℓ∈[1,…,L]\ell\in[1,\ldots,L] as 𝐩(ℓ,t)∈ℝE\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{E}. Since MoE inference routes each token to exactly KK experts, we define a binary request vector 𝐫(ℓ,t)∈[0,1]E\mathbf{r}^{(\ell,t)}\in\mathbb{[}0,1]^{E} by selecting the Top-KK entries of 𝐩(ℓ,t)\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}. We additionally define a soft cache state for token tt at layer ℓ\ell as 𝐜(ℓ,t)∈ℝ≥0E\mathbf{c}^{(\ell,t)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{E} and initialize each 𝐜(ℓ,0)\mathbf{c}^{(\ell,0)} as 𝟎\mathbf{0}. We update this cache state using an exponentially-decayed history of past requests to approximate a recency-weighted cache. Let γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in\left[0,1\right] be a decay factor and CC be the cache capacity. We first compute an un-normalized update according to the following rule

𝐜(ℓ,t+1)=γ​𝐜(ℓ,t)+𝐫(ℓ,t)\mathbf{c}^{(\ell,t+1)}\;=\;\gamma\mathbf{c}^{(\ell,t)}+\mathbf{r}^{(\ell,t)}

During an initial “cache fill” phase, we allow ‖𝐜(ℓ,t)‖1\|\mathbf{c}^{(\ell,t)}\|_{1} to grow until it reaches CC. After this point, we normalize 𝐜(ℓ,t)\mathbf{c}^{(\ell,t)} for subsequent tokens so that ‖𝐜(ℓ,t)‖1=C\|\mathbf{c}^{(\ell,t)}\|_{1}=C is preserved

𝐜(ℓ,t+1)=γ​Z(t)​𝐜(ℓ,t)+𝐫(ℓ,t)Z(t+1),Z(t+1)=γ​Z(t)+KC\mathbf{c}^{(\ell,t+1)}\;=\;\frac{\gamma Z^{(t)}\mathbf{c}^{(\ell,t)}+\mathbf{r}^{(\ell,t)}}{Z^{(t+1)}},\ Z^{(t+1)}\;=\;\gamma Z^{(t)}+\frac{K}{C}

where Z(t)Z^{(t)} is a scalar normalizer that maintains ‖𝐜(ℓ,t)‖1=C\|\mathbf{c}^{(\ell,t)}\|_{1}=C and Z(1)Z^{(1)} is initialized to 11. Alternatively, one can also initialize using a uniform vector with ‖𝐜(ℓ,1)‖1=C\|\mathbf{c}^{(\ell,1)}\|_{1}=C to avoid the initial cache fill phase. In experiments, we set γ=0.9\gamma=0.9, but provide ablation studies for the impact of γ\gamma and CC on throughput in Appendix D.6 and D.7. As γ\gamma controls how long previous routing decisions persist in the cache, smaller values such as γ=0\gamma=0 make the cache more reactive and closer to a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache. In contrast, larger values of γ\gamma such as γ=1\gamma=1 allow previous routing decisions to remain relevant over long horizons in a manner similar to a Least Frequently Used (LFU) cache.

The cache simulation loss can then be calculated as

ℒc​s=1L​T​∑ℓ=1L∑t=1T∑i=1E𝐫i(ℓ,t)​(1−𝐜i(ℓ,t))⏟cache miss proxy at token t, layer ℓ\mathcal{L}_{cs}\;=\;\frac{1}{LT}\sum\limits_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum\limits_{t=1}^{T}\hskip-25.00003pt\underbrace{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{E}\mathbf{r}_{i}^{(\ell,t)}\left(1-\mathbf{c}_{i}^{(\ell,t)}\right)}_{\text{\normalsize cache miss proxy at token $t$, layer $\ell$}} (4)

since a value of 11 for 𝐫i(ℓ,t)\mathbf{r}_{i}^{(\ell,t)} means the router has selected expert 𝐄i(ℓ)\mathbf{E}_{i}^{(\ell)} while a higher value of 1−𝐜i(ℓ,t)1-\mathbf{c}_{i}^{(\ell,t)} means that it is less likely that 𝐄i(ℓ)\mathbf{E}_{i}^{(\ell)} is already in the GPU-resident cache.

Rank Matching Loss ℒr​m\mathcal{L}_{rm}.

The second auxiliary objective is a rank matching loss that aligns the relative routing preferences of the fine-tuned model with the preferences of the original base model. We change the notation slightly from the previous paragraph and refer to the base model’s router distribution for token tt at layer ℓ\ell as 𝐩b(ℓ,t)\mathbf{p}_{b}^{(\ell,t)} and the fine-tuned model’s router distribution as 𝐩f(ℓ,t)\mathbf{p}_{f}^{(\ell,t)}. We count “mistakes” in the fine-tuned model’s ordering as

m(ℓ,t)=∑i,j∈[E]𝕀{𝐩b,i(ℓ,t)>𝐩b,j(ℓ,t)}[ρ−(𝐩f,i(ℓ,t)−𝐩f,j(ℓ,t))]+m^{(\ell,t)}=\sum\limits_{i,j\in\left[E\right]}\mathbb{I}\!\left\{\mathbf{p}_{b,i}^{(\ell,t)}>\mathbf{p}_{b,j}^{(\ell,t)}\right\}\left[\rho-\left(\mathbf{p}_{f,i}^{(\ell,t)}-\mathbf{p}_{f,j}^{(\ell,t)}\right)\right]_{+}

where the operation [a]+:=max⁡(0,a)\left[a\right]_{+}:=\max(0,a). In simple terms, if the base model is more likely to route to an expert 𝐄i(ℓ)\mathbf{E}_{i}^{(\ell)} over 𝐄j(ℓ)\mathbf{E}_{j}^{(\ell)}, then the fine-tuned model should also prefer 𝐄i(ℓ)\mathbf{E}_{i}^{(\ell)} over 𝐄j(ℓ)\mathbf{E}_{j}^{(\ell)} up to some margin ρ\rho. This way, the amount that the fine-tuned model prefers 𝐄i(ℓ)\mathbf{E}_{i}^{(\ell)} over 𝐄j(ℓ)\mathbf{E}_{j}^{(\ell)} is only nominally factored into the loss, but the underlying ordering still matters. The rank matching loss is calculated as

ℒr​m=1L​T​∑ℓ=1L∑t=1Tm(ℓ,t)\mathcal{L}_{rm}\;=\;\frac{1}{LT}\sum\limits_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum\limits_{t=1}^{T}m^{(\ell,t)} (5)

From this, we have the full loss calculation for fine-tuning

ℒ=ℒn​l​l+λc​s​ℒc​s+λr​m​ℒr​m\mathcal{L}\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{nll}\;+\;\lambda_{cs}\mathcal{L}_{cs}\;+\;\lambda_{rm}\mathcal{L}_{rm} (6)

where ℒn​l​l\mathcal{L}_{nll} is the Negative Log-Likelihood loss used in standard language modeling applications. These loss functions jointly reshape routing in a way that is aligned with memory-constrained inference. ℒc​s\mathcal{L}_{cs} promotes within-sequence routing locality by directly penalizing excessive cache transfers, while ℒr​m\mathcal{L}_{rm} prevents router collapse by encouraging the fine-tuned router to preserve the base model’s relative expert preferences. To further highlight the utility of these specific loss functions, we provide brief theoretical justifications for both loss functions in Appendix C. Because we aim for fine-tuning to be memory-efficient, we update only the router parameters, specifically the router weights and gate projection, and apply low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [13] to the MLP up and down projections.

3.1.2  Expert Activation Predictor

In prior offloading systems, learning an expert activation predictor often provides only marginal benefit because routing is noisy, so prefetched experts are evicted before they can be reused. In melinoe, however, fine-tuning induces stronger prompt-conditioned structure in routing, as activations are more consistent per prompt. Motivated by contextual sparsity [21, 12], we learn a prompt-conditioned predictor of expert preferences, Ψ\Psi.

The activation predictor is trained on a dataset generated in the following fashion. For each prompt 𝐪\mathbf{q}, we compute a fixed-dimensional representation using an embedding model ΨEMB\Psi_{\text{EMB}} such that ΨEMB​(𝐪)∈ℝdEMB\Psi_{\text{EMB}}(\mathbf{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{EMB}}}. To construct targets for the activation predictor, we generate a response from the MoE and record router probabilities, 𝐩(ℓ,t)∈ℝE\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{E}, for each token and layer. The supervised target for the predictor is the per-layer average router probability vector defined as

y(ℓ)(𝐪)=1T∑t=1T𝐩(ℓ,t),Y(𝐪)=[y(1)(𝐪)⋯y(L)(𝐪)]y^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{q})\;=\;\frac{1}{T}\sum\limits_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)},\ Y(\mathbf{q})=\left[y^{(1)}(\mathbf{q})\cdots y^{(L)}(\mathbf{q})\right]

where Y⁡(𝐪)∈ℝL×EY(\mathbf{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times E}. This yields a dataset of pairs {ΨEMB​(𝐪n),Y⁡(𝐪n)}n=1N\{\Psi_{\text{EMB}}(\mathbf{q}_{n}),Y(\mathbf{q}_{n})\}_{n=1}^{N}. We train a lightweight two-layer MLP ΨMLP:ℝdEMB→ℝL×E\Psi_{\text{MLP}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{EMB}}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{L\times E} to predict Y^​(𝐪)\widehat{Y}(\mathbf{q}) whose rows [Y^​(𝐪)]ℓ[\widehat{Y}(\mathbf{q})]_{\ell} estimate the layerwise expert preference scores. We normalize the ground truth targets and train ΨMLP\Psi_{\text{MLP}} by minimizing the KL divergence between the normalized target distribution [Y⁡(𝐪)]ℓ[Y(\mathbf{q})]_{\ell} and the predicted distribution by applying a row-wise softmax to [Y^​(𝐪)]ℓ[\widehat{Y}(\mathbf{q})]_{\ell}. Because melinoe reduces routing noise by amplifying prompt-specific expert preferences, even a relatively small ΨEMB\Psi_{\text{EMB}} suffices to produce a lightweight yet accurate predictor. Thus, we enable accurate prefetching, with minimal prefetching latency, and consequently reduce CPU-GPU transfers in the process.

3.2  Post-Deployment Stage

In the post-deployment stage, the fine-tuned MoE and the activation predictor are executed on a memory-constrained device. Given a prompt 𝐪\mathbf{q}, we predict per-layer expert activations by calculating the following using the trained MLP

ΨMLP​(ΨEMB​(𝐪))=Y^​(𝐪)\Psi_{\text{MLP}}(\Psi_{\text{EMB}}(\mathbf{q}))=\widehat{Y}(\mathbf{q}) (7)

For each layer ℓ∈[1,…,L]\ell\in[1,\ldots,L], we form a prefetch set c(ℓ,1)=Top-​C​([Y^​(𝐪)]ℓ)c^{(\ell,1)}=\text{Top-}C([\widehat{Y}(\mathbf{q})]_{\ell}) where CC is the cache capacity. We proactively load the corresponding experts into the GPU-resident cache before generation begins. To increase effective cache capacity, all expert weights are maintained in HQQ INT4, allowing more experts to remain resident in limited GPU memory. Experts that are not resident in GPU VRAM remain in CPU DRAM and are stored in pinned memory to accelerate transfers from CPU to GPU. Transfers are additionally non-blocking, which ensures asynchronous transfers of experts and minimizes PCIe overhead. These offloaded experts are fetched on demand when selected by the router, evicting cached experts as dictated by the cache policy. Overall, melinoe localizes routing through fine-tuning, predicts the resulting per-sequence locality, and exploits it via proactive prefetching and quantized cache residency to reduce cache misses, transfers, and transfer-induced stalls during generation. In the following section, we demonstrate the effectiveness of these various design elements.

4  Results

4.1  Experimental Setup

Models and Datasets.

We evaluate melinoe on three MoE backbones that span size and granularity: OLMoE (77B params.), Phi-3.5-MoE (4242B params.), and Mixtral-8x7B (4747B params.). We train the activation predictor using fixed-dimensional representations from BGE-Base-EN-v1.5 (109109M params.) [30] with embedding dimension 768768. We fine-tune and evaluate across two complementary workloads. We fine-tune on Dolly15K [4] (general instruction-following dataset) and GSM8K [3] (math reasoning with longer generations) and benchmark on held-out evaluation splits.

Fine-Tuning Hyperparameters.

Across all models, melinoe updates the router weights and gate projection layers and applies LoRA rank r=32r=32 to the MLP up and down projections. Remaining weights are fixed at their pretrained initialization. For the cache-simulation loss ℒc​s\mathcal{L}_{cs}, we adopt a deliberately restrictive cache capacity to emphasize the intended deployment regime, setting the simulated cache budget to C=E4C=\frac{E}{4} (e.g. C=16C=16 for OLMoE). We fix the cache decay parameter to γ=0.9\gamma=0.9 and the rank matching margin to ρ=0.1\rho=0.1 throughout. Optimizer settings and fine-tuning hyperparameters are provided in Appendix B.2.

Hardware and Inference Configuration.

We validate performance gains across multiple GPU types: H100 (80GB VRAM), A100 (40GB VRAM), and RTX 4090 (24GB VRAM). To ensure that comparisons reflect realistic memory-constrained deployments, even on larger-memory accelerators, we artificially cap per-process GPU memory using PyTorch limits. We allocate 3GB for OLMoE, 16GB for Phi-3.5-MoE, and 24GB for Mixtral-8x7B. The expert cache uses an LFU eviction policy. Sensitivity to cache size and alternative budgets is deferred to Appendix D.4.

4.2  Main Results

We validate the performance of melinoe against five prior baselines: Fiddler [16], Mixtral-Offloading [10], Deepspeed-MoE [23], FLoE [39], and MoE-Infinity [31]. Across every configuration, melinoe significantly improves throughput relative to the baseline methods (Figure 3). Using OLMoE, melinoe achieves 22.1622.16-23.3223.32 tokens/s on the H100 setup and 15.9915.99-17.1717.17 tokens/s on the RTX 4090 setup. In comparison, the best competing baseline achieves only 14.1914.19-14.6214.62 tokens/s on the H100 setup (FLoE) and 7.617.61-9.449.44 tokens/s on the RTX 4090 setup (Fiddler). These improvements persist with the larger architectures. Phi-3.5-MoE reaches 14.3414.34-15.6715.67 tokens/s on the A100 setup whereas the next closest baselines (Fiddler and Mixtral-Offloading) only attain 5.115.11-5.815.81 tokens/s. Ultimately, MELINOE improves over the best competing baseline by 1.21.2-3×3\times and yields substantially larger gains against baselines that incur frequent weight transfers. For instance, melinoe achieves a 14.7×14.7\times throughput gain over Deepspeed-MoE when using Mixtral-8x7B on the RTX 4090 setup, showing considerable improvements on resource-constrained hardware configurations.

Crucially, melinoe’s throughput gains do not come at the expense of task performance (Table 2). Note that the Fiddler, DeepSpeed-MoE, and MoE-Infinity baselines do not change the base model weights and therefore have the same performance as the base model. On Dolly15K, melinoe achieves the best ROUGE-L with OLMoE (0.24860.2486), Phi-3.5-MoE (0.22700.2270), and Mixtral-8x7B (0.23610.2361). On GSM8K, melinoe again attains the highest accuracy across all three architectures, with the most pronounced improvement occurring with Mixtral-8x7B where melinoe outperforms the next closest baseline by 4.35%4.35\%. Tilting routing towards more persistent per-sequence experts can maintain or even improve quality on the downstream task.

4.3  Ablation Studies and Additional Analysis

Relative Impact of Fine-Tuning vs. Prefetching.

First, we aim to disambiguate the influence of fine-tuning and prefetching on the performance of melinoe. Table 3 quantifies the impact of these disparate components for OLMoE and Mixtral-8x7B on Dolly15K and GSM8K. We conclude that the primary factor in throughput improvements is fine-tuning, which can substantially reduce the number of CPU-GPU transfers. In OLMoE, fine-tuning the model can result in 3×3\times fewer transfers relative to the base model. For Mixtral-8x7B, this reduction in transfer counts is especially valuable as transfers are slow in coarse-grained MoE architectures where experts themselves are larger. Even with PCIe 55 x1616, a single expert transfer for Mixtral-8x7B without quantization can take 55-66 ms. Prefetching provides supplementary benefits, but the improvements are marginal relative to the gains achieved through fine-tuning alone. Nonetheless, prefetching itself takes roughly 0.050.05 seconds but can still reduce end-to-end latency by up to 0.80.8 seconds.

Contribution of Loss Functions on Performance.

Our fine-tuning objective uses two weighting coefficients, λc​s\lambda_{cs} and λr​m\lambda_{rm}, to control the relative influence of the auxiliary losses. Figure 4 exhibits the significance of these terms on the resulting fine-tuned model’s behavior. When holding λc​s=1.0\lambda_{cs}=1.0 and varying λr​m\lambda_{rm}, perplexity is largely stable for moderate values λr​m∈{0.01,0.1,1.0}\lambda_{rm}\in\{0.01,0.1,1.0\} while transfers rise slightly from 278278 to 314314 transfers per layer. When holding λr​m=1.0\lambda_{rm}=1.0 and varying λc​s\lambda_{cs}, increasing λc​s\lambda_{cs} predictably reduces transfers, confirming that the transfer penalty stabilizes expert residency. However, pushing λc​s\lambda_{cs} too high sharply harms the fine-tuned model’s quality, indicating that aggressively minimizing transfers can over-constrain routing and degrade performance. Figure 4 highlights that moderate λc​s\lambda_{cs} and λr​m\lambda_{rm} is an effective balancing point between the objectives, simultaneously achieving large expert transfer reductions while minimally impacting perplexity.

Effect of Batch Size.

We study the impact of batched decoding in Figure 5. We do not include prior offloading baselines as they do not specifically test regimes with batch size >1>1. For melinoe, the activation predictor pools the most likely experts across all sequences in the batch, while all other aspects of the caching policy remain identical to the batch size =1=1 setting. melinoe yields significant throughput gains over the base model and maintains increasing throughput as batch size grows. The relative speedups modestly diminish at larger batch sizes as sequence diversity increases the union of requested experts and induces additional transfers. Fine-tuning to amplify prompt-specific expert preferences remains valuable for memory-constrained MoE inference in multi-request settings.

Effect of Output Generation Length.

A key observation is that fine-tuning does not over-constrain the model and lead to larger performance drops over longer generations. In Table 4, we present the performance of the fine-tuned model at different generation lengths for all three model architectures. Across various output token lengths, the fine-tuned model remains performant. This suggests that melinoe preserves output quality as generation length increases, rather than trade long-horizon stability for short-context gains. Importantly, this supports the view that the cache simulation loss remains viable for variable-length generations.

Coupling Fine-Tuning with Previous Baselines.

Since the fine-tuning procedure in melinoe is not contingent on specific prefetching, quantization, or sparsity schemes, the fine-tuned model checkpoint can be used as a stand-in for the base model when using prior baselines. Table 5 shows that the fine-tuned model checkpoint can improve the throughput of cache-based methods like FLoE and Mixtral-Offloading. Using the same VRAM restrictions as Section 4.2, swapping the base MoE model for the fine-tuned version can yield improvements of up to 5.495.49 tokens/s. Therefore, the fine-tuning procedure proposed in melinoe can be used to augment prior and future offloading baselines.

5  Conclusion

We present melinoe, a procedure that makes MoE models more deployment-friendly under tight VRAM budgets. melinoe fine-tunes an MoE model to strongly prefer a small subset of experts on a per-sequence basis. With these stronger and more consistent expert preferences, caching the preferred experts in GPU memory yields substantially fewer expert transfers during decoding, improving throughput without sacrificing output quality on downstream tasks.

We identify three areas for future work. First, we aim to conduct studies with larger-scale fine-tuning on general-purpose corpora. While we evaluate generalization (Appendix D.1), future work should explore whether this approach is valuable for deploying MoE models across diverse tasks. Second, our current design uses the same number of cached experts per layer, whereas layer-wise cache budgets may provide increased flexibility. Finally, for very long generations, dynamically adapting cache sizes over time may be beneficial. Overall, we view melinoe as a step towards deployment-ready MoE models that retain strong quality while operating efficiently under real hardware constraints.

Appendix A Related Works

Mixture-of-Experts Model Architectures.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model architectures were first proposed as an alternative to traditional transformer-based models [25]. In MoE models, the Feed Forward Network (FFN) present in each transformer block is separated into multiple FFNs which are sparsely activated on a per-token basis. These sparse activations allow MoE models to increase model capacity without a proportional increase in training compute, since only a small subset of experts is executed per token [18, 11, 9, 24]. A few design choices are critical for making MoE models effective in practice. First, expert granularity controls the size and number of experts in the MoE model. Coarse-grained MoE models such as Mixtral-8x7B [15], Phi-3.5-MoE [1], and DBRX [27] all use a relatively small number of large experts. In contrast, fine-grained MoE architectures such as OLMoE [22], Qwen2MoE [33], Qwen3MoE [32], DeepSeek-V2 [6], and DeepSeek-V3 [7] use a higher number of small experts to increase expert specialization and reduce training costs. Another axis by which MoE models differ is their token routing strategy. Initial MoE model architectures such as GShard [18] and GLaM [9] employ router load balancing losses to ensure all experts are utilized in training to prevent expert collapse and token dropping from overloaded experts. BASE Layers [19] instead formulates routing as a linear assignment problem, ensuring experts receive an equal number of tokens during generation. Expert Choice Routing [38] allows each expert to instead pick its Top-KK tokens. More recent works such as Loss-Free Balancing [28] add expert-wise biases to the router’s decisions and update these biases throughout generation to achieve approximate load balancing without an auxiliary loss term. Granularity and routing are critical design choices in downstream deployments as they directly shape the tradeoff between capacity, efficiency, and serving latency.

On-Device Mixture-of-Experts.

The proliferation of open-source MoE models has made on-device deployments of MoEs a critical research direction. MoE inference is often memory-bound since all experts must be accessible at inference time despite their sparse activations. In turn, on-device settings are particularly challenging for MoEs since these devices often have limited GPU memory. In this regime, expert offloading techniques have emerged as a promising way of managing the memory constraints imposed by MoE models. Edge-MoE [35] assumes a highly constrained setting that requires offloading quantized experts to disk memory. However, the following works allow for a larger amount of GPU VRAM and enough CPU DRAM to host all offloaded model weights. Mixtral-Offloading [10], which operates in this more lenient regime, uniformly quantizes experts to 33 bits and all remaining weights to 44 bits, allowing for a larger number of experts to remain resident in GPU DRAM. This variable bit-width quantization incurs additional compute overhead and a non-negligible decrease in model performance. FLoE [39] similarly uses quantization and activation sparsity to increase the size of the GPU-resident expert set but applies them to specific layers where they find compression techniques have the least effect on performance. Other techniques avoid lossy compression schemes and exploit other avenues for reducing I/O latency. MoE-Infinity [31] prefetches experts by profiling previous expert activations and uses KK-means to identify experts that are likely to be activated for a specific request. FineMoE [36] aims to improve on this prefetching scheme by creating expert maps that track token-level activation patterns to prefetch experts in every iteration. An alternative approach proposed by Fiddler [16] is to directly move intermediate activations to CPU memory and perform expert computation on the CPU for CPU-resident experts. As activations are smaller than the expert weights themselves, this method trades compute efficiency for a reduction in I/O latency. Methods such as HarMoEny [8] and Faster MoE [34] which target the multi-GPU inference setting aim to optimize communication but are not directly applicable to this resource-constrained setting.

Routing and Semantic Locality.

While expert offloading is a promising direction for reducing the memory demands of MoE models, recent works suggest that naïvely applying expert offloading may lead to substantial hidden I/O latency. Concretely, MoE models may exhibit low local routing consistency [20], where nearby tokens may activate different experts. This diversity in activations increases the number of cache transfers, reducing the efficacy of a GPU-resident expert set. Recent literature approaches the issue of routing locality in various ways. Oracle-MoE [37] pretrains MoE architectures to route tokens based on attention score-based semantic similarity in order to reduce expert transfers. However, its evaluation is limited to GPT-2-scale models, leaving open how well the approach extends to modern MoE models, where larger architectures and tighter GPU memory budgets can make offloading and transfer bottlenecks more pronounced. BlockFFN [26] similarly performs MoE pretraining but utilizes an auxiliary loss function that encourages neighboring tokens to activate similar experts. BlockFFN does not specifically target expert offloading and only mentions speculative decoding as a device-side acceleration technique that composes with their method.

Appendix C Loss Function Design Justification

In this section, we provide theoretical justification for the choice of our loss functions. Throughout the section, we will use bb and ff in the subscript to associate symbols with the base model and the fine-tuned model respectively, 𝐱=[𝐱1,…,𝐱T]\mathbf{x}=[\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{T}] refers to the sequence of tokens, and Top-​C​(⋅)\textup{Top-}C(\mathbf{\cdot}) refers to an operation that returns a vector with L1L_{1} norm CC and entries 11 for CC positions with the highest magnitude and 00 otherwise. [N][N] for any natural number N∈ℤ+N\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} denotes the set [1,…,N][1,\ldots,N].

C.1  Choice of ℒc​s\mathcal{L}_{cs}

The cache simulation loss ℒc​s​(𝐱)\mathcal{L}_{cs}(\mathbf{x}) is designed to penalize expert activation patterns with excessive switching. Previous work indicates that certain MoE models activate similar experts across adjacent tokens, while others consistently activate a small subset of experts across the decoding trajectory for a given prompt. In the former case, an LRU cache eviction policy is preferable, whereas in the latter an LFU-based eviction policy is more appropriate under conventional caching frameworks.

By fine-tuning the router layers, we can control the underlying expert activation distribution, allowing us to tailor the distribution towards a specific cache eviction policy. The ℒc​s\mathcal{L}_{cs} loss encourages tokens to have similar activation distributions. The decay parameter γ\gamma weights older requests relative to newer ones when computing this similarity. In the following proposition, we will first explain how γ\gamma can be used to interpolate between LFU and LRU updates with hard cache states.

Definition C.1 (γ\gamma cache eviction).

For any given sequence of tokens 𝐱=[𝐱1,…,𝐱T]\mathbf{x}=[\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{T}], let 𝐫f(ℓ,t)​(𝐱)∈{0,1}E\mathbf{r}_{f}^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x})\in\{0,1\}^{E} denote the binary request vector at layer ℓ\ell and token position tt with ‖𝐫f(ℓ,t)​(𝐱)‖1=K\|\mathbf{r}_{f}^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x})\|_{1}=K. From Lemma C.4, one can observe that minimizing the loss ℒc​s​(f)\mathcal{L}_{cs}(f) entails maximizing the terms ϕf(ℓ)​(t,i):=𝔼𝐱∼𝒟train[⟨𝐫f(ℓ,t)​(𝐱),𝐫f(ℓ,i)​(𝐱)⟩]\phi_{f}^{(\ell)}(t,i):=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}\left[\left\langle\mathbf{r}_{f}^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{r}_{f}^{(\ell,i)}(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle\right] which encourages the expert request distributions at layer ℓ\ell for token positions tt and ii to be similar. C.2  Choice of ℒr​m\mathcal{L}_{rm}

Given a sequence of tokens 𝐱=[𝐱1,…,𝐱T]\mathbf{x}=[\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{T}], the purpose of the term ℒr​m​(𝐱)\mathcal{L}_{rm}(\mathbf{x}) is to discourage router collapse onto a small subset of experts. A broadly adopted strategy for preventing distributional collapse while retaining desirable properties of the base model is KL-regularization. Incorporating a KL penalty is ubiquitous across domains including safety fine-tuning, RLHF, knowledge distillation, and reasoning model training where it serves as a general mechanism for constraining policy updates relative to the base model. In our setting, let 𝐩f(ℓ,t)​(𝐱)\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{f}(\mathbf{x}) and 𝐩b(ℓ,t)​(𝐱)\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{b}(\mathbf{x}) denote the router distributions at layer ℓ\ell and token position tt induced by the fine-tuned and base routers, respectively. One may then define the KL loss as follows

ℒr​mKL(𝐱,f)=1L​T∑ℓ=1L∑t=1TKL(𝐩f(ℓ,t)(𝐱)∥𝐩b(ℓ,t)(𝐱)).\mathcal{L}_{rm}^{\textup{KL}}(\mathbf{x},f)=\frac{1}{LT}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\textup{KL}\left(\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{f}(\mathbf{x})\|\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{b}(\mathbf{x})\right).

Although this may be a natural choice in tasks such as knowledge distillation where the objective is to match the teacher’s distribution, our setting is different. We are less concerned with divergence between the two distributions in the KL or entropy sense and are ultimately interested in the induced rankings, since the model selects the Top-KK experts from the router distribution. We, therefore, choose a loss that is more directly aligned with mismatches in the induced rankings. Concretely, we model this using the Kendall rank correlation coefficient [17].

Definition C.7.

Given two router output distributions 𝐩,𝐪∈ΔE\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{E}, the Kendall rank correlation coefficient τ⁡(𝐩,𝐪)∈[−1,1]\tau(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})\in[-1,1] is defined as

τ⁡(𝐩,𝐪)=1−2​Inv​(𝐩,𝐪)(n2),\tau(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})=1-\frac{2\textup{Inv}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})}{{n\choose 2}},

where Inv​(𝐩,𝐪)\textup{Inv}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}) is the number of pairwise inversions between distributions 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐪\mathbf{q}.

Maximizing the rank correlation coefficient is equivalent to minimizing the inversion number. Ideally, one could use the following loss function

ℒr​minv​(𝐱)=1L​T​∑ℓ=1L∑t=1TInv​(𝐩f(ℓ,t)​(𝐱),𝐩b(ℓ,t)​(𝐱)).\mathcal{L}_{rm}^{\textup{inv}}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{LT}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\textup{Inv}\left(\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{f}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{b}(\mathbf{x})\right).

Note that when this loss is 00, the experts activated by the fine-tuned router and the base router will be exactly the same. However, the term Inv​(⋅,⋅)\textup{Inv}(\cdot,\cdot) is difficult to parameterize and differentiate with respect to the parameters of the fine-tuned model ff. One can express the inversion number as follows

Inv​(𝐩f(ℓ,t)​(𝐱),𝐩b(ℓ,t)​(𝐱))=∑i,j∈[E]gb(ℓ,t)​(𝐱,i,j)​gf,Inv(ℓ,t)​(𝐱,i,j),\textup{Inv}\left(\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{f}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{b}(\mathbf{x})\right)=\sum\limits_{i,j\in\left[E\right]}g_{b}^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x},i,j)\;g_{f,\textup{Inv}}^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x},i,j),

where

gb(ℓ,t)(𝐱,i,j):=𝕀{𝐩b,i(ℓ,t)(𝐱)>𝐩b,j(ℓ,t)(𝐱)}andgf,Inv(ℓ,t)(𝐱,i,j):=𝕀{𝐩f,i(ℓ,t)(𝐱)<𝐩f,j(ℓ,t)(𝐱)}.\displaystyle g_{b}^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x},i,j):=\mathbb{I}\!\left\{\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{b,i}(\mathbf{x})>\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{b,j}(\mathbf{x})\right\}\quad\text{and}\quad g_{f,\textup{Inv}}^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x},i,j):=\mathbb{I}\!\left\{\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{f,i}(\mathbf{x})<\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{f,j}(\mathbf{x})\right\}.

To facilitate learning using gradient-based methods, we use m(ℓ,t)m^{(\ell,t)} as a proxy for the inversion number Inv​(⋅,⋅)\textup{Inv}(\cdot,\cdot). Specifically, we replace gf,Invg_{f,\textup{Inv}} by gfg_{f}, i.e.,

m(ℓ,t)​(𝐱)=∑i,j∈[E]gb(ℓ,t)​(𝐱,i,j)​gf(ℓ,t)​(𝐱,i,j)withgf(ℓ,t)​(𝐱,i,j):=[ρ−(𝐩f,i(ℓ,t)​(𝐱)−𝐩f,j(ℓ,t)​(𝐱))]+m^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x})=\!\!\!\!\!\sum\limits_{i,j\in\left[E\right]}g_{b}^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x},i,j)\;g_{f}^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x},i,j)\quad\textup{with}\quad g_{f}^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x},i,j):=\left[\rho-\left(\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{f,i}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{f,j}(\mathbf{x})\right)\right]_{+} (12)

and define ℒr​m\mathcal{L}_{rm} as

ℒr​m​(𝐱,f)=1L​T​∑ℓ=1L∑t=1Tm(ℓ,t)​(𝐱).\mathcal{L}_{rm}(\mathbf{x},f)=\frac{1}{LT}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}m^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x}).
Lemma C.8.

Define m(ℓ,t)(𝐱)=∑i,j∈[E]𝕀{𝐩b,i(ℓ,t)(𝐱)>𝐩b,j(ℓ,t)(𝐱)}[ρ−(𝐩f,i(ℓ,t)(𝐱)−𝐩f,j(ℓ,t)(𝐱))]+m^{(\ell,t)}(\mathbf{x})=\sum\limits_{i,j\in\left[E\right]}\mathbb{I}\!\left\{\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{b,i}(\mathbf{x})>\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{b,j}(\mathbf{x})\right\}\left[\rho-\left(\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{f,i}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{p}^{(\ell,t)}_{f,j}(\mathbf{x})\right)\right]_{+} as in Equation (12). Remark C.9.

As a consequence of Lemma C.8, minimizing loss ℒr​m\mathcal{L}_{rm} is equivalent to maximizing a lower bound on the rank correlation coefficient between the fine-tuned and base router expert request distributions averaged across layers ℓ∈[L]\ell\in[L] and token positions t∈[T]t\in[T].

Appendix D Additional Experiments

D.1  Out-of-Distribution Generalization Performance of melinoe

As mentioned in Section 5, computational constraints prevented us from performing large-scale fine-tuning on a comprehensive, general-purpose dataset. Such training would likely yield a more deployment-friendly model that reduces inference latency across a wider range of downstream tasks. Instead, we evaluate whether melinoe continues to provide throughput improvements when the fine-tuning data used in the pre-deployment stage and the downstream task differ.

In Table 11, we consider the same settings and resource constraints highlighted in Sections 4.1 and 4.2. We find that even when the fine-tuning dataset and downstream task differ fundamentally, the throughput improvements relative to prior baselines persist but are partially dampened. For example, when evaluated on a holdout of Dolly15K, Phi-3.5-MoE fine-tuned exclusively on GSM8K still achieves 10.4410.44 tokens/s, 1.861.86 tokens/s greater than Mixtral-Offloading, the next best baseline. However, this is still slower than the 14.3414.34 tokens/s achieved when Phi-3.5-MoE is fine-tuned on Dolly15K itself. Mixtral-8x7B can remarkably achieve 8.218.21 tokens/s when fine-tuned on GSM8K and evaluated on a holdout of Dolly15K, only 1.141.14 tokens/s less than when it is fine-tuned on Dolly15K. Similarly, when Mixtral-8x7B is fine-tuned on Dolly15K, its decoding throughput is only 2.132.13 tokens/s less on GSM8K then a model fine-tuned on in-distribution data. This suggests that the improvements present in melinoe are largely preserved even when the resource-constrained device in question has a particularly different local data distribution. We hope that future work can better demonstrate melinoe’s generalizability on various downstream tasks by performing more diverse pre-deployment fine-tuning and downstream evaluation.

D.2  Effect of Output Generation Length on Throughput

As output length increases, melinoe maintains stable throughput (Figure 6), which suggests that the fine-tuned model’s expert preferences endure even in longer generations. In this regime, memory-efficiency becomes increasingly critical as the KV cache grows with the number of generated tokens, leaving less room for resident experts. Despite this, melinoe sustains near constant tokens/s, indicating that its routing stability reduces cache churn over long decoding horizons.

D.3  Impact of Fine-Tuning on Expert Routing

Figures 7, 8, and 9 demonstrate the effects of fine-tuning on expert activations for OLMoE, Phi-3.5-MoE, and Mixtral-8x7B, respectively. Across all model architectures, fine-tuning skews activations towards a few highly preferred experts, justifying fine-tuning as a meaningful approach to make routing more predictable for MoE models. Additionally, Figure 10 demonstrates that routing still remains diverse across multiple sequences, suggesting that the combined effect of the fine-tuning procedure presented in melinoe is to create sequence-specific skew but retain global expert usage diversity.

D.4  Ablation on GPU VRAM Budget

Figure 11 displays the impact of GPU VRAM on decoding throughput. Across all VRAM budgets, melinoe outperforms prior offloading baselines, demonstrating its robustness across a diverse array of downstream deployments.

D.5  Ablation on Quantized Experts

Quantizing experts to HQQ INT4 allows more experts to remain in GPU VRAM. In Table 12, we analyze the effects of quantization on throughput. Each setting has roughly equal GPU VRAM usage. Quantization improves throughput, but its benefit is not proportional to the increase in resident experts due to compute overhead. The fine-tuned model with 88 resident experts has greater throughput than the quantized base model with 2424 resident experts.

D.6  Ablation on Soft Cache Capacity in Loss

In Figure 12, we evaluate the effect of the soft cache capacity used in fine-tuning on the average number of transfers per layer in the downstream evaluation. We consider three different cache budgets during evaluation, C=16C=16, C=32C=32, and C=48C=48. Performance is noticeably worse when the soft cache capacity is set too low as transfers are dominated by forced evictions, making subtle routing choices more difficult to learn. There is also a slight degradation in the number of transfers when the soft cache budget is set too high as few transfers occur in this regime so transfer penalties remain limited.

D.7  Ablation on Loss Function Decay Factor

Figure 13 studies the decay factor γ\gamma used in the cache simulation loss, which controls how long past expert usage is factored into current eviction decisions. We find that transfers are high when γ\gamma is too small but decrease rapidly as γ\gamma increases across all cache budgets. Thus, overly aggressive decay makes routing decisions too myopic when using an LFU eviction policy.

D.8  Ablation on Cache Eviction Policy

Finally, in Table 13, we quantify the impact of the cache eviction policy on the number of transfers per layer. For smaller values of γ\gamma, an LRU policy results in fewer cache transfers as the model was fine-tuned with a more reactive cache simulation loss. However, using a larger γ\gamma with an LFU policy results in the fewest number of transfers overall.
